actions.name: Camera inspection of submandibular/neck swelling
actions.result: Firm, warm, diffusely swollen area bilaterally beneath the mandible, more pronounced on the right, extending toward midline and down toward the hyoid region. Skin appears taut and slightly shiny. No fluctuance appreciated visually. Patient reports it is tender to light self-palpation.

actions.name: Floor of mouth inspection via camera
actions.result: Patient tilts phone light into mouth: floor of mouth appears elevated and tongue is pushed up/back slightly. Limited visualization due to trismus; patient unable to open more than ~2 fingerbreadths.

actions.name: Maximal interincisal opening (patient self-measured with fingers)
actions.result: Patient reports approximately 2 fingerbreadths (~20-25 mm) between upper and lower incisors; pain with further attempted opening.

actions.name: Home/reported temperature
actions.result: 38.6°C (101.5°F) oral, taken this morning per patient report.

actions.name: Voice and swallowing assessment
actions.result: Voice sounds muffled/'hot potato' quality on call. Patient reports pain and difficulty swallowing his own saliva and is drooling intermittently. He is sitting upright and says lying flat feels worse.

actions.name: Work of breathing observation
actions.result: No visible stridor or accessory muscle use on camera at rest; respiratory rate appears normal by observation. Patient states breathing feels 'okay' but endorses needing to sit up to feel comfortable.

actions.name: Review prior panoramic radiograph (14 months old)
actions.result: Panoramic image shows deep carious lesion in tooth #30 (mandibular right first molar) extending to the pulp with an associated periapical radiolucency approximately 6mm in diameter. No radiograph available for other teeth of concern.

actions.name: Review current medication list
actions.result: Metformin 1000 mg twice daily (diabetes); ibuprofen 800 mg every 4 hours for 2 days (patient-directed, exceeds recommended OTC/Rx max dosing frequency); amoxicillin 500 mg capsules, source and remaining course unknown, taken intermittently from a relative's leftover prescription.

actions.name: Review most recent HbA1c result
actions.result: HbA1c 9.1% (H), drawn 2 months ago, indicating poorly controlled type 2 diabetes.

actions.name: Camera inspection of neck for erythema/skin changes
actions.result: Mild diffuse redness over the submandibular area bilaterally, no obvious skin breakdown, crepitus cannot be assessed remotely.

actions.name: Lymph node self-palpation guidance
actions.result: Patient reports tender, firm, enlarged nodes under the right jaw when gently pressing per instruction; unable to distinguish nodes from diffuse swelling.

actions.name: Airway risk stratification
actions.result: Documented as high-risk spreading odontogenic infection with bilateral submandibular space involvement, trismus, dysphagia, muffled voice, and fever — consistent with early Ludwig's angina presentation. Airway compromise risk assessed as significant and time-sensitive.

actions.name: Decision for disposition (ED vs. routine dental appointment)
actions.result: Determined that this presentation requires immediate emergency department evaluation for airway management and IV antibiotics; outpatient dental antibiotic prescribing or scheduling a routine extraction visit is not appropriate given current signs.

actions.name: Hydration/drooling assessment
actions.result: Patient reports needing to spit frequently and some drooling; says he is still able to swallow his own saliva, slowly and with pain.

actions.name: Review dental insurance/coverage status
actions.result: No dental insurance on file; patient has previously deferred care due to cost.

actions.name: Camera inspection of tooth #30 region intraorally
actions.result: Limited view due to trismus; posterior right mandibular area appears inflamed, large carious lesion partially visible on the back molar, surrounding gum tissue reddened. Unable to fully visualize due to limited opening.

artifacts.title: Panoramic Radiograph Report
artifacts.author: Dr. A. Thibodeaux, DDS (prior dental office)
artifacts.body:
PANORAMIC RADIOGRAPH, dated 14 months prior to current visit.

FINDINGS: Tooth #30 (mandibular right first molar) demonstrates extensive coronal caries with radiographic involvement of the pulp chamber. A periapical radiolucency measuring approximately 6 mm in diameter is present at the mesial root apex, consistent with chronic periapical periodontitis/early abscess formation. No other significant periapical pathology noted on remaining dentition. Mandibular cortex grossly intact; no obvious widening of mandibular canal.

IMPRESSION: Nonrestorable/advanced carious lesion tooth #30 with periapical pathology. Extraction or endodontic therapy recommended at time of imaging; patient did not return for treatment.

objectives.text: Recognize signs and symptoms of a spreading odontogenic infection with impending airway compromise (bilateral submandibular swelling, trismus, dysphagia, muffled voice, fever, throat tightness when supine) consistent with early Ludwig's angina.
Correlate current presentation with prior radiographic findings to identify the likely odontogenic source of infection.

Identify medication-related safety concerns including excessive ibuprofen dosing frequency and inappropriate self-medication with leftover antibiotics, and recognize poorly controlled diabetes as a risk factor for infection severity.

Make an appropriate urgent disposition decision within scope: recognize this requires immediate emergency department referral rather than antibiotic prescribing or routine scheduling, and communicate this clearly despite patient's stated goals.
Elicit and explore sensitive psychosocial barriers (cost concerns, work pressures, healthcare avoidance) with empathy while still prioritizing patient safety.
Identify the discrepancy between the patient's belief that his breathing is fine and clinical/historical evidence suggesting early airway risk.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states his breathing is 'okay' and does not report any breathing difficulty.
mismatches.recordEvidence: The symptom progression shows a sharp spike in swelling severity overnight (0 to 3 on a 0-3 scale) concurrent with new trismus, muffled voice, and dysphagia -- a pattern of rapid clinical progression that is a known precursor to airway compromise regardless of the patient's subjective reassurance about breathing.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients with early airway-threatening infections may subjectively feel their breathing is fine even as objective signs (rapid swelling progression, trismus, dysphagia, need to sit upright) indicate imminent risk. Clinical judgment and trend data must override patient self-assessment of breathing adequacy in this context.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports taking leftover amoxicillin from a relative hoping it would treat his infection.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication list documents the amoxicillin source and course as unknown/unverified, taken only intermittently 'a few times' over 2 days -- an inadequate, unsupervised antibiotic course that would not reliably treat a spreading infection and may have contributed to a false sense of reassurance that masked symptom progression.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-medication with leftover or incomplete antibiotic courses can inadequately treat an infection, potentially altering symptom presentation while the underlying process continues to spread -- this is not an effective substitute for proper diagnosis and treatment, and reinforces the clinician's duty to disclose that this does not constitute adequate care.

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in New Orleans, Louisiana
profile.summary: A 48-year-old line cook with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents via teledentistry video visit with a 5-day history of a right mandibular molar toothache that paradoxically improved the day before new bilateral submandibular swelling, trismus, dysphagia, and muffled voice developed overnight -- a classic pattern for a spreading odontogenic infection with airway risk (Ludwig's angina) arising from an untreated carious/abscessed tooth #30. This case teaches dental students to recognize red-flag signs of airway-threatening dental infection in a remote visit, correctly weigh patient-reported reassurance against objective trend data, and make the scope-appropriate decision to refer immediately to emergency care rather than prescribing antibiotics or scheduling routine treatment.
profile.title: Rapidly Progressive Submandibular Swelling and Trismus Following Untreated Molar Abscess

answerKey.primaryProblem: Spreading odontogenic infection (submandibular space, bilateral) secondary to untreated periapical abscess of tooth #30, with early signs concerning for Ludwig's angina and impending airway compromise.
differential: Early Ludwig's angina / bilateral submandibular space infection from odontogenic source (most likely)
Unilateral submandibular (Vincent's) space abscess without bilateral spread
Sialadenitis or submandibular gland infection (less likely given dental source and radiographic correlation)
Reactive cervical lymphadenitis alone (does not explain trismus, dysphagia, muffled voice)
Peritonsillar abscess (less likely given exam findings localized to submandibular/jaw region and dental source)
keyFindings: 5-day history of right mandibular molar pain that improved just before new overnight swelling -- a pattern suggesting the infection decompressed from the tooth into surrounding soft tissue spaces
Firm, bilateral submandibular swelling extending toward midline
Subjective throat tightness when attempting to lie flat, preference for sitting upright
Prior panoramic radiograph (14 months ago) confirming deep caries and periapical radiolucency at tooth #30, untreated
HbA1c 9.1% indicating poorly controlled diabetes, a risk factor for rapid infection spread and poor healing
Inadequate self-treatment with excessive-frequency ibuprofen and an incomplete, unsupervised course of leftover amoxicillin
plan: Advise immediate emergency department evaluation today -- do not delay for a dental appointment or outpatient antibiotic trial

Clearly explain to patient that this presentation (bilateral swelling, trismus, muffled voice, dysphagia, fever) carries risk of airway obstruction and requires same-day emergency assessment, possible IV antibiotics, and surgical drainage
Advise patient to stop relying on leftover/borrowed antibiotics and not to attempt to manage this with over-the-counter analgesics alone

Instruct patient to call 911 or go immediately to the nearest ED if he develops worsening difficulty breathing, inability to swallow saliva, increasing drooling, or difficulty speaking at all while en route
Communicate empathetically about cost/work concerns while being firm that this is a time-sensitive, potentially life-threatening situation that takes priority
Document findings in a Dental SOAP note and arrange communication/handoff information for the ED team including prior radiograph findings and antibiotic history
Plan for follow-up dental treatment (likely extraction or root canal of tooth #30) only after the acute infection and airway risk have been addressed in the emergency/hospital setting
Encourage patient to also establish ongoing diabetes management given HbA1c of 9.1%, as this is a modifiable risk factor for future infection severity, with primary care follow-up
redFlags: Bilateral submandibular swelling extending toward midline
Trismus with limited mouth opening (~2 fingerbreadths)
Patient-reported throat tightness when supine, preference for upright positioning
Rapid overnight progression of swelling following initial pain improvement (suggests spread rather than resolution)
Fever with chills in setting of poorly controlled diabetes
educationPoints: A decrease in tooth pain does not always mean improvement -- it can indicate that infection has decompressed into surrounding soft tissue spaces, which may be a sign of worsening, not resolving, disease.

Trismus, muffled voice, dysphagia, and drooling together are red-flag signs of a spreading deep space infection and possible impending airway compromise, and warrant emergency referral regardless of the patient's own breathing assessment.
Poorly controlled diabetes (reflected by elevated HbA1c) is a significant risk factor for rapid progression and severity of odontogenic infections.

Self-medication with leftover or incomplete antibiotic courses, and excessive-frequency NSAID dosing, are not substitutes for definitive treatment and can mask or delay recognition of a worsening infection.

Teledentistry providers must recognize when a presentation exceeds the scope of outpatient dental management and requires immediate escalation to emergency medical care rather than prescribing or scheduling routine follow-up.
Addressing patient concerns about cost and missed work with empathy, while still clearly conveying urgency, supports both patient trust and safety.
